newsitem.title: UK: Some N Irish peace talks obstacles removed - Adams.
newsitem.headline: Some N Irish peace talks obstacles removed - Adams.

text.p: British and Irish ministers on Friday welcomed a statement by Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams in which he said the two governments had removed some obstacles to meaningful negotiations on Northern Ireland's future.

The statement was issued jointly by Adams, whose party is the political wing of the IRA, and John Hume, leader of the province's largest Catholic party, the Social Democratic and Labour Party, after talks on Thursday.
"It is our view that the peace process can be restored and that with political will on all sides we can move towards a new political agreement," the two men said.

They said Britain under the Conservatives had erected "obstacles to an inclusive and meaningful negotiations process", but added: "We welcome the moves that have been made to remove these obstacles by the new Irish and British governments.
The Labour Party won a landslide election victory in Britain on May 1 and a Fianna Fail coalition took over the reins of government in Dublin a few weeks later.

Asked whether the statement would help efforts to establish peace in the province, Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam told journalists: "I hope it is a precursor, but I think we will have to wait and see where we go from that statement."

She was speaking after a three-hour meeting in London with Irish Foreign Affairs Minister Ray Burke to discuss the two governments' efforts to maintain the momentum towards substantive all-party talks on the future of Northern Ireland.

"Obviously I welcome the (Hume-Adams) statement," Burke said. "I hope that we will have an early restoration of the unequivocal (Irish Republican Army) ceasefire and I hope it will be sooner rather than later."

The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February last year, resuming its 28-year-old armed struggle for a united Ireland. Britain and Ireland insist it must lay down its arms again if it is to join all-party talks on the future of the province.
The two governments are facing anger from pro-British Protestant parties over their conditions for allowing Sinn Fein into these talks, which are due to resume in September.
Mowlam on Thursday night made public a letter she wrote on July 9 to Sinn Fein chief negotiator Martin McGuinness.

In it she said once Sinn Fein called a ceasefire and entered talks, it could remain in them provided it respected principles of non-violence and democracy set out by their chairman, former U.S. senator George Mitchell.
But the negotiations would proceed alongside discussions about the "decommisioning" of weapons held by the Irish Republican Army and other guerrilla groups.

David Trimble, leader of Northern Ireland's largest Protestant party, the Ulster Unionists, told British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday these ideas would not put enough pressure on the IRA to disarm.

"It is absolutely essential from our point of view that there are clear commitments to actual disarmament that will be endorsed by the British government, the Irish government and all the parties to the negotiations," he told reporters after a stormy meeting with Blair.
Burke said the two governments would look at any amendments to these ideas which Trimble might table before they are voted on by Northern Irish parties other than Sinn Fein on Wednesday.
But, standing on the steps of the building where his meeting with Mowlam took place, he added: "This document has been very carefully crafted."
"No message should go from these steps to give any indication that anything is going to be allowed, or any individual is going to be allowed, to come between the two governments on this issue."
If Protestant parties vote against the proposals for decommissioning on Wednesday, the whole talks strategy could be in jeopardy.
